nodes.label: The Sasanian Empire
nodes.full: The Persian empire founded by Ardashir I, ruling Iran and Mesopotamia — the imperial power that governs the Arabian coast as provinces, garrisons and colonises it, holds the Gulf trade route, and whose fall to the Arab conquest ends the whole order.
nodes.src: background — see the sassanid-224-484 and sassanid-484-651 folios

nodes.label: The Church of the East (Ctesiphon)
nodes.full: The Christian church of the Persian empire, headed by the Catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon — the hierarchy that organises the Gulf as the ecclesiastical province of Beth Qatraye, holds the synods its bishops attend, and whose authority the Gulf church rejects for a generation.
nodes.src: background; the Synodicon Orientale

nodes.label: Muhammad and the community at Medina
nodes.full: The Prophet Muhammad and the young Muslim state at Medina — the source of the letters and envoys that bring the Gulf into Islam by negotiation, and of the movement that within thirty years absorbs the entire Sasanian Empire.
nodes.src: background — see the caliphate-632-750 folio

nodes.label: The Sasanian province system on the Arabian shore
nodes.full: After Ardashir's conquest the Sasanians governed the Arabian coast as provinces — Mishmahig on Bahrain, Hagar in the al-Hasa oasis, Mazun in Oman — each under a marzban with Persian garrisons and settlers.
nodes.src: the Šahrestānīhā ī Ērānšahr; al-Tabari; Potts (1990) vol.2

nodes.label: The Julanda dynasty rules Oman under Persian suzerainty
nodes.full: The Azdi house of Julanda held the Omani interior as kings, acknowledging Sasanian overlordship on the coast but running the mountains and oases themselves — the pattern of a strong interior and a foreign-influenced coast that recurs throughout Omani history.
nodes.src: al-Awtabi's "Ansab al-Arab"; Wilkinson, "The Imamate Tradition of Oman" (1987)

nodes.label: Al-Mundhir ibn Sawa accepts Islam in Bahrain
nodes.full: The Sasanian-appointed governor of Bahrain, al-Mundhir ibn Sawa of the Banu Tamim, received a letter from the Prophet Muhammad and converted, bringing eastern Arabia into the Muslim community by agreement rather than conquest.
nodes.src: Ibn Sa'd's "Tabaqat"; al-Baladhuri's "Futuh al-Buldan"

nodes.label: Jayfar and Abd al-Julanda bring Oman into Islam
nodes.full: The brothers Jayfar and Abd, joint Julanda rulers of Oman, accepted Islam after receiving the Prophet's envoy Amr ibn al-As. Oman's peaceful entry into Islam, without a caliphal army, underlies its later insistence on governing itself.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri, "Futuh al-Buldan"; al-Awtabi

nodes.label: Eastern Arabia governed from Basra
nodes.full: Under the Umayyads and early Abbasids, Bahrain and Oman were administered as appendages of Basra, their governors appointed by the Iraqi viceroy. Distance from the centre made both regions chronically hard to hold.
nodes.src: al-Tabari and al-Baladhuri on the Basran governorship

nodes.label: Al-Julanda ibn Masud, first imam of Oman
nodes.full: As the Umayyad state collapsed, the Omani Ibadis elected al-Julanda ibn Masud as imam — the first attempt to realise their ideal of a community governed by an elected, deposable religious leader. An Abbasid army killed him within two years.
nodes.src: al-Salimi, "Tuhfat al-Ayan"; Wilkinson (1987)

nodes.label: Shapur II's campaign against the Arabs
nodes.full: Shapur II, called 'Dhu'l-Aktaf' for the way he punished captives, campaigned across eastern Arabia against tribes raiding into Iran, storming Hajar and deporting whole populations. It fixed Sasanian dominance over the Arabian shore for three centuries.
nodes.src: al-Tabari I.836-839 (Bosworth)

nodes.label: The Ridda war in Bahrain — the siege of Juwatha
nodes.full: On the Prophet's death much of Bahrain renounced Islam under al-Hutam and a claimant king. The Muslim loyalists, chiefly the Abd al-Qays, were besieged at Juwatha until a relief force under al-Ala al-Hadrami broke the revolt.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on the Ridda in al-Bahrayn

nodes.label: The Battle of Dibba
nodes.full: The Omani apostasy under Laqit ibn Malik, 'Dhu al-Taj', ended at Dibba, where a caliphal army with Julanda allies destroyed the rebel host. A vast early cemetery at Dibba is traditionally linked to the dead of the battle.
nodes.src: al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari on the Omani Ridda

nodes.label: The Abbasid conquest of Ibadi Oman
nodes.full: An Abbasid expeditionary force under Khazim ibn Khuzayma crushed the first Ibadi imamate at Julfar, killing Imam al-Julanda ibn Masud. Ibadi self-government in Oman would have to be rebuilt from scratch a generation later.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Khazim ibn Khuzayma's campaign; al-Salimi

nodes.label: Sasanian military colonisation of the Gulf coast
nodes.full: The Sasanians planted Persian cavalry colonists (later the 'Asawira') and deported Arab tribes to develop the al-Hasa and Bahrain oases under the marzban's tax administration. The eastern Arabian coast became, in effect, an Iranian frontier province.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Shapur II's deportations; al-Baladhuri on the Asawira

nodes.label: The Synod of Dayrin, 676 — canons for the Gulf churches
nodes.full: The Catholicos George I sailed to Tarut island and held a synod for the bishops of Beth Qatraye, issuing nineteen canons on clergy, marriage, inheritance and the conduct of women — and healing a decades-long schism.
nodes.src: Acts of the Synod of Mar George (676), Synodicon Orientale

nodes.label: The Beth Qatraye schism
nodes.full: For nearly thirty years the bishops of the Gulf refused obedience to the Catholicos in Ctesiphon, running their church as an autonomous body. The dispute — over authority, not doctrine — shows how far the Gulf Christian community had grown into its own identity.
nodes.src: the schism and its 676 resolution (Synodicon Orientale); Brock, ARAM 11-12 (1999-2000)

nodes.label: The Prophet's letter to al-Mundhir and the dhimma of Bahrain
nodes.full: The settlement with al-Mundhir ibn Sawa let the Zoroastrians, Jews and Christians of Bahrain keep their religion in return for the jizya tax. It is one of the earliest worked examples of the protected-minority arrangement that would govern non-Muslims across the caliphate.
nodes.src: Ibn Sa'd, "Tabaqat" I; al-Baladhuri; Morony (1984)

nodes.label: Sasanian fire worship on the Arabian shore
nodes.full: The Persian garrisons and settlers brought Zoroastrian fire ritual to the Gulf coast. Fire-holders and Sasanian religious imagery appear in the archaeology, and later Muslim writers remember 'Majus' among the population of Bahrain and Oman.
nodes.src: Sasanian material from Gulf sites; the 'Majus' in the dhimma settlement (Ibn Sa'd)

nodes.label: The bishoprics of Beth Qatraye
nodes.full: From at least 410, the Church of the East organised the Gulf as the province of Beth Qatraye, with bishops on Bahrain, at Tarut, in the al-Hasa oasis, on the Trucial coast and in Oman. Christianity was the majority faith of the settled Gulf population for two centuries.
nodes.src: Synods of 410, 424, 544, 576, 676 (Synodicon Orientale)

nodes.label: The Gulf monasteries — Sir Bani Yas, Al-Qusur, Kharg
nodes.full: A string of courtyard monasteries with plastered churches, monks' cells and moulded crosses ran down the Gulf islands. The Sir Bani Yas monastery, founded around 600 and abandoned peacefully in the 8th century, is the best preserved.
nodes.src: Sir Bani Yas (King, BSOAS 60, 1997); Al-Qusur on Failaka

nodes.label: Isaac of Nineveh and the Qatari ascetic tradition
nodes.full: Isaac the Syrian, the most widely read spiritual writer the Church of the East produced, was born in Beth Qatraye. His treatises on prayer, solitude and divine mercy were later translated into Greek, Arabic, Ethiopic and Slavonic and are read across Christianity to this day.
nodes.src: Isaac of Nineveh, 'Ascetical Homilies'; Kozah et al. (2014)

nodes.label: Jewish communities of eastern Arabia and Oman
nodes.full: Jewish groups lived in the al-Hasa oasis and in Oman through the Sasanian and early Islamic periods, named among the protected communities of the region and remembered in local tradition — one strand of the Gulf's pre-Islamic religious plurality.
nodes.src: 'Jews' among the dhimmis of al-Bahrayn (Ibn Sa'd); al-Baladhuri

nodes.label: The mosque of Juwatha
nodes.full: Tradition holds that the Abd al-Qays built a mosque at Juwatha soon after accepting Islam, and that it was the first place outside Medina where the Friday congregational prayer was held. Its ruined remains are among the oldest mosque sites in the Gulf.
nodes.src: Juwatha mosque tradition in the hadith collections and al-Bakri

nodes.label: The plaster crosses of Sir Bani Yas
nodes.full: The Sir Bani Yas church was decorated with moulded gypsum panels — crosses on stepped bases, vine scrolls, rosettes — in a style shared with Church-of-the-East sites in Iraq. It is the finest late-antique Christian art surviving in the Gulf.
nodes.src: Sir Bani Yas stucco corpus (King, BSOAS 60, 1997)

nodes.label: Courtyard-monastery and church plans
nodes.full: The Gulf monasteries share a plan: a single-aisle church with a raised sanctuary, ranged around a courtyard with cells, a refectory and cisterns. The uniformity shows a connected monastic movement working to a common template.
nodes.src: Carter, "Christianity in the Gulf during the first centuries of Islam", AAE 19 (2008)

nodes.label: The Sasanian torpedo jar
nodes.full: Tall, pointed, bitumen-lined storage jars — 'torpedo jars' — are the signature container of the Sasanian and early Islamic Gulf, carrying dates, wine and fish sauce. Sherds of them trace Persian Gulf trade all the way to Sri Lanka and China.
nodes.src: Kennet, "Sasanian and Islamic pottery from Ras al-Khaimah" (2004)

nodes.label: The earliest Gulf mosques
nodes.full: The first Gulf mosques were simple mud-brick prayer halls, their qibla walls later fitted with concave mihrabs. The transition can be read on the ground where a monastery is abandoned and a mosque rises in the same oasis within a generation.
nodes.src: Juwatha mosque; early Omani mosque archaeology; Carter (2008)

nodes.label: Dadisho Qatraya on the solitary life
nodes.full: Dadisho of Qatar wrote commentaries on the ascetic classics and a treatise on solitude that codified the theory of the hermit's life for the whole Church of the East.
nodes.src: Dadisho Qatraya, 'On Stillness'; Kozah et al. (2015)

nodes.label: Gabriel of Qatar's liturgical commentary
nodes.full: Gabriel of Qatar wrote the earliest full commentary on the Church of the East's daily services, explaining the meaning of every prayer and rite. It is a primary source for how Christians actually worshipped in the late-antique Gulf.
nodes.src: Gabriel of Qatar, 'Commentary on the Liturgical Offices'; Brock's edition

nodes.label: A cluster of scholars from one small region
nodes.full: Within a single century Beth Qatraye produced Isaac of Nineveh, Dadisho, Gabriel, Ahob the exegete and Abraham bar Lipeh — an intellectual output out of all proportion to the region's size, and evidence of a real network of Gulf monastic schools.
nodes.src: Brock, ARAM 11-12 (1999-2000); the 2014-15 Qatar edition project

nodes.label: Cosmas Indicopleustes on the Persian Christians of the sea
nodes.full: The merchant-monk Cosmas records a bishop 'appointed from Persia' and a full Christian clergy on Sri Lanka, and Persian Christian traders along the whole route. The Gulf church was one node in a Christian network reaching to India and beyond.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes, 'Christian Topography' 3.65 and 11

nodes.label: The Persian Gulf as the Sasanian trade artery
nodes.full: While Byzantium's eastern trade ran through the Red Sea, the Sasanian Empire's ran up the Gulf. Persian ships and merchants — many of them Christians of the Church of the East — dominated the sea route to Sri Lanka and reached the ports of south China.
nodes.src: Cosmas Indicopleustes; Procopius on the 'silk war'

nodes.label: Sohar rises as the gateway to China
nodes.full: Sohar grew in this period into the greatest port of the Omani coast, later remembered as 'the hallway of China and the storehouse of the East'. Its rise made the Batinah coast the economic centre of gravity of southern Arabia.
nodes.src: Sohar excavations (Kervran; Whitehouse); al-Muqaddasi

nodes.label: The pearl fishery under Persian rule
nodes.full: Sasanian and early Islamic sources continue to name the Gulf's pearls as a prime luxury. The industry ran without interruption through the change of empires — the divers and the merchant fleets outlasting every state that claimed to govern them.
nodes.src: pearls of al-Bahrayn in the early Arabic geographers

nodes.label: Persian oasis development in al-Hasa
nodes.full: The Sasanians invested in the al-Hasa oasis — its springs, canals and date gardens — settling deportees and colonists to farm it. It became the agricultural anchor of the eastern Arabian province and stayed the region's breadbasket for centuries.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on Shapur II's development and settlement of Hajar

nodes.label: Julfar and the northern Oman coast
nodes.full: The town at Kush near Julfar shows continuous occupation from the Sasanian into the Islamic period as a minor port and pearling base — the ancestor of the Julfar that would dominate the lower Gulf a thousand years later.
nodes.src: Kennet, "Sasanian and Islamic Pottery from Ras al-Khaimah" (2004)

nodes.label: Sasanian deep-water shipping
nodes.full: Persian shipwrights built the sewn-plank vessels that carried Gulf trade to Sri Lanka and China on the monsoon. The technology — no iron nails, hulls stitched with coir and sealed with bitumen and fish oil — remained the Gulf standard into the 20th century.
nodes.src: Agius, "Classic Ships of Islam" (2008)

nodes.label: Monastic water systems on the islands
nodes.full: The island monasteries survived on carefully built cisterns, wells and rainwater channels — the same problem the Neolithic islanders had faced, solved with late-antique engineering. Water management was the precondition for a contemplative life on a desert island.
nodes.src: water installations at Sir Bani Yas and Al-Qusur; Carter (2008)

nodes.label: The aflaj maintained through the imperial changes
nodes.full: The Iron Age falaj systems of Oman kept flowing through Sasanian and early Islamic rule, their upkeep organised by the oasis communities regardless of who governed the coast. Continuity of the water infrastructure meant continuity of settlement.
nodes.src: Wilkinson, "Water and Tribal Settlement in South-East Arabia" (1977)

nodes.label: The Church of the East as an Indian Ocean network
nodes.full: Beth Qatraye's bishops travelled to synods in Iraq; its monks and traders carried the faith to the Malabar coast, Socotra and Sri Lanka. The Gulf was a link in a Christian chain that stretched, along the trade routes, from Syria to south China.
nodes.src: Synodicon Orientale; Cosmas Indicopleustes; the Church of the East's Asian mission

nodes.label: Syriac and Arabic in the Gulf schools
nodes.full: The Qatari writers worked in Syriac but lived among Arabic-speakers; within a century their world would be Arabic-speaking and Muslim. Their works became a bridge — several were translated into Arabic and fed into the wider Islamic-era spiritual literature.
nodes.src: the Arabic reception of Isaac of Nineveh and Dadisho; Brock

nodes.label: The Azd of Oman migrate to Basra
nodes.full: Large numbers of the Omani Azd resettled in the new garrison city of Basra, becoming one of its dominant tribal blocs and a power in early Islamic politics. Oman's affairs and Basra's were thereafter entangled for centuries.
nodes.src: the Azd of Basra in al-Tabari; Wilkinson (1987)

nodes.label: The Prophet's envoys reach the Gulf
nodes.full: Letters and envoys from Medina to al-Mundhir ibn Sawa in Bahrain and the Julanda brothers in Oman brought both regions into Islam by negotiation. The Gulf's entry into the new order was diplomatic before it was military.
nodes.src: the Prophet's letters preserved in the sira and hadith literature

nodes.label: Byzantium and Persia divide the Indian Ocean trade
nodes.full: The long Byzantine-Sasanian rivalry had a maritime dimension: Byzantium worked the Red Sea and courted Ethiopia and Yemen, while Persia held the Gulf. Eastern Arabia's prosperity depended on the Gulf route staying the winning one.
nodes.src: Procopius, 'Wars' 1.19-20; the Aksumite-Himyarite wars as a proxy struggle

nodes.label: The Sasanians conquer Yemen
nodes.full: Khosrow I sent a force that overthrew the Ethiopian regime in Yemen and made it a Persian province. For a few decades Persia controlled both ends of Arabia — the Gulf and the Bab al-Mandab — and the whole peninsula's trade.
nodes.src: al-Tabari on the Persian conquest of Yemen and the governorship of Wahriz

nodes.label: The rise of Islam and the Arab conquest of Persia
nodes.full: Within thirty years the new Muslim state absorbed the whole Sasanian Empire. For the Gulf coast it meant the Persian governing apparatus vanished and the region became part of a polity centred, for the first time in a millennium, on Arabia and then Iraq.
nodes.src: al-Qadisiyya (636), Nihawand (642); the death of Yazdegerd III (651)

nodes.label: The founding of Basra reorients the Gulf
nodes.full: The new garrison city of Basra became the administrative and naval capital of the Gulf, from which Bahrain and Oman were governed and toward which their tribes and trade were drawn. The Gulf's centre of gravity moved to its head.
nodes.src: foundation of Basra under Umar, 638 (al-Baladhuri)

nodes.label: The Abbasid revolution
nodes.full: The overthrow of the Umayyads convulsed the whole caliphate. In the confusion the Omani Ibadis proclaimed their first imam — and the victorious Abbasids, once secure, sent an army to destroy him.
nodes.src: Sharon, "Black Banners from the East" (1983)

nodes.label: The solitary as a recognised way of life
nodes.full: Dadisho Qatraya's treatise 'On Stillness' gives the hermit — withdrawn, silent, outside ordinary social and family roles — a fully theorised place in the church. The Gulf helped define solitude itself as a legitimate human vocation.
nodes.src: Dadisho Qatraya, 'On Stillness / Shelya'; Brock

nodes.label: The 676 canons on women in church
nodes.full: Several of the Synod of Dayrin's canons concern women — barring them from certain parts of the church, regulating consecrated virgins and widows, restricting mixed gatherings. The rules are restrictive, but they document an active female presence the hierarchy felt the need to control.
nodes.src: Canons of the Synod of Mar George (676), Synodicon Orientale

nodes.label: The dead of Dibba
nodes.full: The very large early cemetery at Dibba — thousands of simple graves — is traditionally the burial of those killed in the Ridda battle. Whatever its exact makeup, it is a rare physical trace of the human cost of the wars that fixed the Gulf inside Islam.
nodes.src: the Dibba cemetery (Sharjah and Fujairah archaeology authorities)

nodes.label: Becoming dhimmi
nodes.full: For the Gulf's Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, the settlements of the 620s created a new legal identity: protected non-Muslims, free to practise but taxed and subordinate. Christianity persisted in the Gulf for generations under this status before fading in the 8th-9th centuries.
nodes.src: the dhimma arrangements (Ibn Sa'd; al-Baladhuri); Carter (2008)
